result: This manuscript describes a registered replication report as part of the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology, which aims to replicate key experiments from Ricci-Vitiani et al. (2010) published in Nature. The project is a collaboration between the Center for Open Science and Science Exchange.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C5 accurately describe the scope and organizational structure of the Reproducibility Project. These are straightforward descriptive claims about the project itself, supported by direct statements in the manuscript and verifiable through the cited organizational affiliations.

result: The original Ricci-Vitiani et al. study demonstrated that glioblastoma stem-like cells can differentiate into endothelial cells and that selective ablation of these tumor-derived endothelial cells using a Tie2-tk/ganciclovir system reduces tumor progression in vivo, while fully differentiated glioblastoma cells cannot form functionally relevant endothelium.
evaluation: Claims C3, C4, and C21-C28 accurately summarize the key findings and experimental approach from the original Ricci-Vitiani et al. study. These claims are supported by direct citations to specific figures from the original publication and describe the experimental design (Tie2-tk system with appropriate controls) and main conclusions that will be replicated.

result: The manuscript establishes the biological context that GBM is a highly aggressive cancer with extensive vasculature, maintained by cancer stem cells that can differentiate into functional endothelium, challenging conventional theories about tumor vasculature origin and offering new therapeutic targets.
evaluation: Claims C6-C14 provide background context supported by appropriate citations (Purhonen et al., 2008; Vescovi et al., 2006; Fan et al., 2013; Ricci-Vitiani et al., 2010; Kaur and Bajwa, 2014). These claims accurately represent established knowledge and the scientific rationale for the replication study.

result: The original Ricci-Vitiani et al. study demonstrated through multiple approaches that tumor-derived endothelial cells in GBM share genetic signatures with tumor cells, that GSCs can differentiate into endothelial cells in culture and in vivo, while fully differentiated glioblastoma cell lines cannot.
evaluation: Claims C15-C20 accurately describe the experimental evidence from the original study, including genetic lineage tracing in patient samples, in vitro differentiation assays, and in vivo xenograft experiments. These claims are properly attributed to Ricci-Vitiani et al. through citations.

result: Multiple independent studies (Wang et al., 2010; Soda et al., 2011; Chiao et al., 2011) have reported findings consistent with Ricci-Vitiani et al., showing that glioblastoma tumors can give rise to tumor-derived endothelial cells with the same genetic signature as the tumor.
evaluation: Claims C29-C32 accurately cite supporting studies that corroborate the main findings of Ricci-Vitiani et al. The citations are appropriate and the described findings align with the original study's conclusions.

result: Contradictory findings from Rodriguez et al. (2012) and Cheng et al. (2013) suggest that GSCs do not give rise to endothelial cells, with Cheng et al. proposing an alternative hypothesis that GSCs differentiate into Tie2-expressing pericytes rather than endothelial cells, which when targeted produce similar anti-tumor effects.
evaluation: Claims C33-C39 accurately describe contradictory findings in the literature with appropriate citations. The alternative pericyte hypothesis is particularly important as it could explain the Tie2-tk targeting results through a different mechanism. The citation to De Palma et al. (2005) for pericyte Tie2 expression is appropriate.

result: El Hallani et al. initially reported GSC transdifferentiation into vascular smooth muscle-like cells, but later work suggested GSCs fuse with endothelial cells to create hybrid vasculature rather than transdifferentiating.
evaluation: Claims C40-C42 accurately describe the evolution of findings from El Hallani et al., showing how their interpretation changed from transdifferentiation to cell fusion. The citations to both 2010 and 2014 publications are appropriate.

result: Additional studies by Lathia et al. (2011) and Ghanekar et al. (2013) failed to observe tumor-derived endothelial cells, with Lathia et al. providing only textual description without data, and Ghanekar et al. finding no evidence in hepatocellular carcinoma.
evaluation: Claims C43-C45 accurately describe negative findings from the literature. The notation that Lathia et al. reported observations without showing data (C44) is an important methodological critique. The extension to hepatocellular carcinoma by Ghanekar et al. provides context about the generalizability of the phenomenon.

result: Protocol 1 will evaluate Tie2 expression in GSC83, U87MG, and HMVEC-d cell lines using qRT-PCR as a quality control step, with three biological replicates and two technical replicates per run, expecting low expression in glioblastoma cells and high expression in endothelial cells.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 clearly describe the experimental design for Protocol 1. The sample size (3 biological × 2 technical replicates) is justified by power calculations showing >80% power. The quality control rationale is appropriate for ensuring baseline Tie2 expression levels before transduction experiments.

result: GSC83 cells will be cultured at 20,000 cells/ml and subcultured every 7 days, which allows for two cell doublings.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 describe standard cell culture procedures for GSC83 cells. The doubling time information is consistent with typical glioblastoma stem cell growth characteristics and provides necessary methodological detail.

result: According to Ricci-Vitiani et al., U87MG cells have 100% tumor incidence with 3-4 week tumor formation time, while GSC83 neurospheres have ~60% tumor incidence with 4-6 month tumor formation time.
evaluation: Claims C53-C56 provide important parameters from the original study that inform experimental design and sample size calculations. The substantial difference in tumor incidence rates (100% vs 60%) and formation times justifies the inclusion of extra mice in the GSC83 cohort.

result: The replication study will use a single-injection model rather than the dual-injection approach described in the original methods section, based on clarification from the original authors that dual injections caused problematic differences in tumor growth rates.
evaluation: Claims C57-C59 identify an important discrepancy between published methods and actual practice in the original study. The authors' clarification that dual injections were problematic is critical information. The decision to use single injections in the replication is methodologically sound and properly justified.
